title: Death’s first offer: sons, herds, land and life
theme: Death tempts the boy away from his question with everything a householder could want: long-lived sons and grandsons, cattle, elephants, gold and horses, a great realm, and as many years as he likes.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «शतं वर्षाणि आयूंषि येषां तान् शतायुषः»

words.meaning: as many as, as long as

sandhi.type: visarga as r; t voiced before a vowel
sandhi.rule: bhūmeḥ before the voiced m shows r (the visarga of a non-a vowel). mahat before a vowel becomes mahad, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).

sandhi.type: aḥ before a voiced consonant; t voiced
sandhi.rule: śaradaḥ before y becomes śarado, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च) with guṇa, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः). yāvat before i becomes yāvad, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).

samasa.meaning: those whose lives are a hundred years; the vigraha is Śaṅkara’s
elephants and gold, taken as one collective (neuter singular); the vigraha is Śaṅkara’s

morphology.note: Accusative plural of śarad ‘autumn’, i.e. ‘years’; the accusative of extent of time.
Imperative middle of vṛ (9th class) ‘choose’; repeated in the next verse.

translation.literal: Choose sons and grandsons living a hundred years, many cattle, elephants and gold, horses; choose a great domain of the earth; and yourself live as many autumns as you wish.
translation.readable: Choose sons and grandsons who will live a hundred years, cattle in plenty, elephants, gold and horses. Choose a great kingdom on the earth, and live yourself for as many years as you like.

anvaya: शतायुषः पुत्रपौत्रान् बहून् पशून् हस्तिहिरण्यम् अश्वान् [च] वृणीष्व । भूमेः महत् आयतनम् वृणीष्व । स्वयम् च यावत् शरदः इच्छसि [तावत्] जीव ।
syntax: Three imperatives, each with its objects: a list for the first (persons, beasts, wealth), one object for the second, and for the third an accusative of time with a relative of measure (śarado yāvad icchasi).

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: a wide domain on the earth, a kingdom — «महत् विस्तीर्णम् आयतनम् आश्रयं मण्डलं साम्राज्यं». Raṅgarāmānuja gives that and an alternative: a great house on the earth, with halls and palaces — «विचित्रशालाप्रासादादियुक्तं गृहं वृणीष्व».

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Triṣṭubh. The half-lines count 22 and 24: the last pāda (svayaṃ ca jīva śarado yāvad icchasi) has 13 syllables, two more than the norm, as the text stands in every witness.

beginner: Death now changes tactics. Instead of arguing, he tempts. Ask for children and grandchildren who will each live a hundred years, he says; ask for herds of cattle, elephants, gold and horses; ask for a great kingdom; and live yourself as long as you want. Everything an ordinary person might dream of is laid in front of the boy. Śaṅkara notes the logic of the last offer: all the rest would be worthless if the boy himself did not live to enjoy it, so Death adds long life too. The commentators agree that this is still the test begun in the last verse: will Naciketas trade his question for comfort?
analogy: Like a recruiter who, when a candidate asks the one question that matters, slides a bigger salary across the table instead of answering.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Long-lived sons and grandsons, many cattle, elephants and gold, horses, a great domain on the earth, and as many years of life as the boy wants.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: having been answered, Death tempts him again — «एवमुक्तोऽपि पुनः प्रलोभयन्नुवाच मृत्युः». Long life is added because the rest would be useless to a short-lived man: «सर्वमप्येतदनर्थकं स्वयं चेदल्पायुरित्यत आह».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Raṅgarāmānuja: the knowledge of the freed self is not to be given to one whose mind is held by other things — «विषयान्तरासक्तचेतसे एतादृशं मुक्तात्मतत्त्वं नोपदेशार्हम्» — so Death tempts him to make his desire for release firm.

advaita.text: A renewed temptation: «एवमुक्तोऽपि पुनः प्रलोभयन्नुवाच मृत्युः». The great domain is a kingdom — «मण्डलं साम्राज्यं».

visistadvaita.text: The temptation keeps the desire for release firm: such knowledge is not fit to be taught to one attached to other things — «विषयान्तरासक्तचेतसे एतादृशं मुक्तात्मतत्त्वं नोपदेशार्हम्».

schools.disagreement: None of substance: both read the offer as a test of fitness for the teaching. Madhva’s bhāṣya on the passage 1.1.22–25 comments only on the ‘do not ask’ of 1.1.25.

parallels.note: The Gītā’s ‘those attached to pleasure and power, their minds carried off by it’, in whom resolute understanding does not arise: the danger Death is testing for.

contemporary.text: The list is the ordinary measure of a successful life — family, assets, property, health and length of days. The verse asks what we would give up a question for, and suggests that the offer itself reveals what the question is worth. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: If someone offered you everything on this list to stop asking one question, would you stop?
reflect.deeper: Why does Death include long life last, after everything else?
reflect.practice: Write down the three things you would most like to have. Then ask what each one would leave unanswered.

flags.note: The vishvAsa mūla lengthens vṛṇīṣva to vṛṇīṣvā (a Vedic lengthening; corrections.json).
